name: Sugarcane extract
lead: Sugarcane extract refers to preparations from Saccharum officinarum used in cosmetics, most often described as a natural source of alpha hydroxy acids, chiefly glycolic acid. Glycolic acid can be isolated from sugarcane and is also found in sugar beets, pineapple, cantaloupe and unripe grapes [1].

Alpha hydroxy acids are used in cosmetics for chemical exfoliation, and glycolic acid is listed among keratolytic agents used for acne [1][2]. The most common side effects of AHAs are mild irritation, redness and flaking, and the FDA has warned that AHAs can raise the likelihood of sunburn, an effect described as reversible when use stops [2]. Skin products labeled "sugarcane extract" vary in what they contain and at what strength.

Separate from cosmetics, a polyphenol-rich sugarcane extract (PRSE) has been studied in cells and animals for antioxidant, metabolic and antiviral effects [3][4][5]. A 2021 anticancer paper on PRSE was retracted [6]. No trial in the sources reviewed tests sugarcane extract for skin appearance.
infobox: Natural source of glycolic acid (an AHA) [1]

paras: Sugarcane is one of the most important sources of sugar and is also rich in polyphenols, with epicatechin identified as a dominant component in one extraction study [7]. In cosmetic marketing, "sugarcane extract" is typically promoted as a plant-derived exfoliant because glycolic acid occurs in the plant, which produces it as part of photosynthetic metabolism [1].

Sugarcane-derived ingredients appear in gentle exfoliating and brightening products. The sources reviewed contain no community discussion. Claims in marketing generally mirror those for AHAs: smoother texture and brighter skin from removal of surface dead cells.

AHAs such as glycolic, lactic, mandelic and citric acid are alpha hydroxy carboxylic acids used for exfoliation [2]. The FDA and the Cosmetic Ingredient Review panel consider AHAs safe when sold at low concentrations, at pH above 3.5, and with sun-protection instructions [2]. Glycolic acid itself is classed as a skin irritant and corrosive at high concentrations in its hazard labeling [1]. How much active acid a given plant extract delivers is not established in the sources reviewed.

PRSE has been reported to show antioxidant activity and effects on carbohydrate-metabolism pathways in cells [3], antifibrotic activity in rats [7], enzyme inhibition relevant to blood sugar [8] and antiviral activity against influenza A in vitro [5]. A paper reporting anticancer effects of PRSE was later retracted [6]. These studies are preclinical.

No studies found on sugarcane extract for skin appearance. Human research on other sugarcane products includes a randomized trial of blackstrap molasses versus polyethylene glycol for pediatric functional constipation [9], and registered trials on sugarcane juice in liver patients and on sugarcane biopolymer wound dressings [10][11]. These concern different products and outcomes.

card.summary: A plant source of glycolic acid pitched as a gentle natural exfoliant; the AHA is well known, the extract itself is untested for skin.
card.aka: Saccharum officinarum extract, natural glycolic acid source
card.note: Acid content of sugarcane extracts is unclear; AHAs can increase sun sensitivity.

quick.overview:
Sugarcane extract is used in skincare chiefly as a plant-derived source of glycolic acid, an alpha hydroxy acid that loosens surface skin cells.

Research on the extract itself is mostly in cells and animals, and no skin-appearance trial appears in the sources reviewed.
quick.mechanism: AHAs act as chemical exfoliants. Separately, polyphenol-rich sugarcane extract shows antioxidant and enzyme-inhibiting activity in lab studies.
quick.risks: AHAs commonly cause mild irritation, redness and flaking, and the FDA has warned they can increase sunburn likelihood. One anticancer paper on the polyphenol extract was retracted.
